ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In order to determine the exit velocity of a toy gun bullet, a group of students from our school took a ping-pong ball, made a small hole in it, and filled it with some modeling clay. They measured the masses of the ball and the bullet using a balance, which were $M$ and $m$ respectively. Then, they placed the ping-pong ball on the edge of a table, loaded and cocked the toy gun, and set it on the table, aiming horizontally at the hole in the ball. After pulling the trigger, the bullet entered the hole and was ejected horizontally along with the ball. The height of the table was $h$, and the horizontal distance from the landing point of the ping-pong ball to the edge of the table was $s$.

1. How can the velocity of the bullet be expressed in terms of the measured quantities?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, the toy gun is located on the left side, and the muzzle points horizontally toward the small ball at the edge of the table; the small ball is labeled with mass M and is located near the edge of the table. After the bullet is shot horizontally from left to right into the small ball, the small ball and the bullet fly out horizontally from the edge of the table together, and the figure uses a dashed line to draw the parabolic trajectory toward the lower right. The vertical height from the tabletop to the ground is labeled h, and the horizontal distance from the landing point to the edge of the table is labeled s. Reasoning: Let the velocity of the bullet when it is shot be u, and the common horizontal velocity after the bullet enters and moves together with the ping-pong ball containing plasticine be V. After the collision, the whole undergoes horizontal projectile motion; in the vertical direction there is h = (1/2)gt^2, so the flight time t = sqrt(2h/g). In the horizontal direction it moves at a constant velocity, with s = Vt, therefore V = s/t = s sqrt(g/(2h)). The collision time is very short, and the impulse of the external force in the horizontal direction can be neglected, so the momentum in the horizontal direction is conserved during the collision: m u = (M + m)V. Substituting V gives u = ((M + m)/m) s sqrt(g/(2h)). Rewriting it equivalently as u = ((M+m)s sqrt(2gh))/(2mh).
